main_issue: The guideline describes missing authorization checks for privileged server-side capabilities, but all listed cases concern unsafe HTML cleaning or sanitization that permits XSS. No anchor or trace evidence shows a lower-privilege caller reaching a privileged server-side effect.
suggested_guideline: Trace user-controlled HTML through parsing, DOM transformation, configured cleaner filters, and final serialization or rendering. Report restricted or security-sensitive cleaning paths where the effective filter chain lacks an element, attribute, URI-scheme, comment, or malformed-input sanitizer; where a sanitizer is applied outside the relevant mode or transformation scope; or where validation accepts markup that downstream rendering interprets as executable content. Confirm the bypass reaches an HTML-rendering sink and that the proposed fix applies an allowlist-based sanitizer to the same parsed representation and restricted-mode path before output. A safe implementation uses explicit element, attribute, and URI-value allowlists, removes unsafe comments or parser artifacts where relevant, and tests malicious markup through the complete configured cleaner pipeline.
evidence_notes: CVE-2019-10219 anchors point to Hibernate Validator SafeHtml validation and tests, which are HTML/XSS sanitization evidence rather than authorization-boundary evidence.

CVE-2023-29201 explicitly identifies a restricted HTML-cleaning path whose default filter chain lacked a sanitizer allowlist filter; the fix activates SanitizerFilter and adds element/attribute/URI checks.

CVE-2023-29528 traces user-controlled HTML through HtmlCleaner, DOM processing, configured filters, and restricted transformations; anchors identify omitted comments and incomplete restricted-mode coverage.

The three cases can support a broad HTML-cleaner/sanitizer-pipeline guideline, although the exact bypass primitive for the Hibernate case is not provided in the payload and should be verified before making a narrower shared claim.
